About: Field Lines — Traced From the Field

Source

Topic
Electrostatics — visualising the electric field
Simulation
Interactive two-charge configuration with live-traced field lines
Concept
Field lines are integral curves of E — the engine WALKS along the field, so where they crowd the field is strong, and they can never cross.
Serves
Distinguishing a dipole (lines run from + to −) from a like-charge pair (no line joins them; E = 0 at a null point on the axis); building the geometric intuition that supports Gauss's law later.
Inquiry
Predict what happens between two LIKE charges before flipping the sign.
Misconception
"Lines are a drawing convention" / "lines could cross where fields are complicated."

Guided Inquiry

1 · Look at the dipole

Two point charges, +q on the left and −q on the right. Every curve on the canvas is a field line: the engine puts a seed near a charge and steps along the local field direction, over and over, until it hits another charge or leaves the frame.

Notice where the lines crowd close together, and where they thin out. That spacing is not artistic — it is what the tracer produced.

2 · Predict — like charges

Right now q₂ is negative and the lines run from + to −. If q₂ is flipped to positive, so both charges are +q, what becomes of the lines that ran from one charge to the other?

3 · Flip the sign and watch

Flip the sign of q₂ with the Sign of q₂ control. Watch the midpoint of the axis joining the charges: compare how the lines run there now with how they ran in the dipole. Flip it back and forth as often as you like.

Every curve is still doing the same thing — starting near a charge and walking along the local field. With two sources, no such walk can end on a charge, so each one turns away and leaves the frame.

4 · Read the local field

A yellow test point appears on the canvas. Drag it. The arrow is the force a +1 test charge would feel, and the number is |E| in natural units (k = 1 — a shape number, not V/m).

Now move the test charge along a single field line. The arrow stays tangent to the line — that is why the curve exists at all.

5 · Crowded lines, strong field

Move the test point outward along one field line, from near a charge to the frame edge. Compare how fast the gaps to neighbouring lines widen with how fast |E| falls.

The convention — lines per unit cross-sectional area ∝ |E| — describes a three-dimensional bundle. This canvas is one flat slice of it, so here the gaps widen in proportion to r while |E| falls as 1/r². Crowded still means strong; the two just do not fall at the same rate.

Field Lines

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two point charges sit on a grid, and the sim draws the electric field around them as a set of curves. Each curve is traced from the field itself, step by step, so you can check the picture against the numbers.

What you'll learn

  • How a field line is built from the electric field E at each point.
  • How the pattern of lines depends on the sign and size of the two charges.
  • What the yellow arrow and the |E| number say about the field at one point.
  • How the spacing of the lines relates to the strength of the field.
q₁ is always positive. q₂ can be either sign. You can drag each charge and the yellow test point.

What's on screen

  • Charges: red for positive, blue for negative, each labelled with its value.
  • Field lines: thin blue curves, each with a small arrowhead showing which way E points.
  • Test point: the yellow dot, with an arrow and a |E| label.
  • At the test point panel: |E| and the arrow's direction in degrees.
See itLook at the start state, a + charge and a − charge. Watch for: thin blue curves, each leaving one charge, with an arrowhead partway along.

03

A field line follows the field

The electric field E at a point is a vector: it has a direction and a size. A field line is the curve whose tangent at every point lies along E there. The sim builds each one by taking short steps of length ds along E:

dr / ds = E / |E|
Each step goes in the direction of E, whatever its size.
  • A line starts on a small circle around a charge and stops when it nears a charge or leaves the frame.
  • The arrowhead points the way E points: away from a + charge, toward a − charge.
  • Lines never cross. E has one value at each point, so there is only one tangent there.
See itPut the yellow point on one of the lines. Watch for: the yellow arrow lying along the blue line it sits on, not across it.
04

Two charges add their fields

Each charge makes its own field, and the field at a point is the vector sum. In the sim's units (k = 1) a charge q at ri contributes q(r − ri) / |r − ri|³, with q signed, so

E = q₁(r − r₁)/|r − r₁|³ + q₂(r − r₂)/|r − r₂|³
The sum is a vector sum: x and y parts add separately.

At the start position of the yellow point, (0.5, 1.2), with q₁ = +1 at (−1, 0) and q₂ = −1 at (1, 0):

sourceExEy
q₁ alone0.2120.169
q₂ alone0.228−0.546
sum0.439−0.377

That is |E| = 0.579, at −40.6° from the +x axis, which is what the panel reads.

See itRead the panel with the yellow point at its start place. Watch for: |E| close to 0.58 and a direction near −41°.
05

Two like charges leave no line joining them

Field lines start on + charges and end on − charges. Flip q₂ to + and both charges are sources, so no line can end on either one. The lines bend away and leave the frame. The one that starts exactly along the axis runs into the null point below and stops.

Between the charges the two fields point opposite ways, so on the axis there is one point where they cancel and E = 0, the null point. It lies at a distance

x = d √|q₁| / (√|q₁| + √|q₂|)
measured from q₁, with d the distance between the charges (2 at the start).
  • Equal charges put it at the midpoint. With |q₁| = 3 and |q₂| = 1 it moves to x ≈ 0.27, nearer the smaller charge.
  • Lines bend away from the null point, so they are sparse around it.
  • Far from both charges the pair looks like one charge q₁ + q₂.
See itMake both charges + and put the yellow point at the midpoint. Watch for: no blue line joining the charges, and |E| reading close to 0 at the midpoint.
06

Crowded lines mean a strong field, but not by the same factor

Where lines crowd together the field is strong, and where they are sparse it is weak. As a comparison between two places in one picture, that always holds. As a ruler it does not, because the canvas is a flat slice.

Take one charge with N = 14|q| lines spread round it. At distance r the gap between neighbouring lines is about 2πr/N, so it grows in proportion to r. The field is |E| = |q|/r², so it falls as 1/r².

one charge, |q| = 1r = 0.5r = 2change
gap between lines0.220.904× wider
|E|4.000.2516× smaller

In three dimensions, lines per unit area fall as 1/r², which matches |E|. The flat slice cannot show that.

See itMove the yellow point straight up from the + charge. Watch for: |E| falling from about 0.9 at 1.0 above the charge to about 0.2 at 2.0 above it.
07

Where it matters

  • Gauss's law. In three dimensions the number of lines leaving a closed surface is proportional to the charge inside it. The sim's 14 lines per unit of |q| follows that rule.
  • Uniform fields. Between two large parallel plates the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced, which says E has the same size and direction everywhere between them.
  • Conductors. In electrostatics, field lines meet the surface of a conductor at right angles.
  • Zero-field points. A charge placed at a null point feels no force from the pair. To find one, set the two fields equal and opposite.
08

Summary

In one line. Field lines are a picture built from the electric field E of the charges, so where they run and how they crowd both come from E.

Key points

  • A field line is tangent to E at every point, and lines never cross.
  • The field of two charges is the vector sum of their single-charge fields.
  • Like charges: no line joins them, and E = 0 at one point.
  • For one charge |E| = |q|/r², but line gaps in a flat slice grow as r.

Common mix-ups

  • "Field lines are just a drawing convention." Here every curve is computed from E.
  • "Lines can cross where the field is complicated." E has one direction at each point. At a null point E is zero and lines bend away.
  • "A charge released from rest follows a field line." It starts moving along the line, but its inertia carries it off any curved line.

Things to try on your own

  • Set both charges + with |q₁| = 3 and |q₂| = 1. Drag the yellow point along the axis to find where |E| reads close to 0.000, and compare with x ≈ 0.27.
  • Keep the dipole and drag the yellow point along one line from + to −, watching |E|.
  • Raise |q₁| from 1 to 3 and note how many more lines leave it.
